Let me try a bipartite approach instead: I'll partition the vertices into A = {0,1,2,3,4,5,6} and B = {7,8,9,10,11,12,13}, which naturally places 4 in A and both 9 and 13 in B, so the required edges stay between the two parts. Since bipartite graphs have no odd cycles, I just need to avoid 4-cycles by ensuring no two vertices in A share more than one neighbor in B. I need to relabel the vertices so that 9 and 13 are in different parts of the bipartition. Let me make 9 a point and 13 a line, then construct the Fano plane with points {0,1,2,3,4,5,9} and lines {6,7,8,10,11,12,13}. I'll define line 13 as {4,9,1} so it contains both 4 and 9, which gives me the edges (4,13) and (9,13) I need. Then I'll assign the remaining six Fano lines to vertices 6 through 12.

Now I'm listing out all the edges from each line: line 7 connects 0, 3, and 4 to vertex 7; line 8 connects 0, 5, and 9 to vertex 8; line 10 connects 1, 3, and 5 to vertex 10; line 11 connects 2, 3, and 9 to vertex 11; line 12 connects 2, 4, and 5 to vertex 12; and line 13 connects 1, 4, and 9 to vertex 13. This gives me 21 edges total, which matches the Heawood graph structure. Since the Fano plane has the property that any two lines intersect in exactly one point, there are no 4-cycles in this bipartite graph, confirming girth 6.
